summary: This document adds an RSA-R mode to MIKEY for cases where the initiator doesn't know the responder's public key or identity ahead of time, as with call forwarding. It also lets group members start a key download themselves. It updates RFC 3830.

eli5.summary: Usually you need someone's lock before sending them a secret. This lets the receiver show their own lock first, so a call can be secured even if you reached the wrong person.

questions: how does mikey handle call forwarding keys
what is the difference between mikey rsa and rsa-r
subtitle: A MIKEY mode where the responder picks the traffic key and proves who it is, for calls that get forwarded and for group key download.

tldr.problem: In MIKEY's public-key mode the Initiator must know the Responder's public key and ID in advance, which fails when a call is forwarded or when group members want to fetch keys on their own.
tldr.mechanism: MIKEY-RSA-R reverses the roles: the Initiator sends a signed request, and the Responder replies with the traffic key, encrypted to the Initiator's public key, together with its own identity or certificate.
tldr.outcome: It adds one full roundtrip, new message types 9 and 10, and error number 13 to MIKEY, and it updates RFC 3830. The Initiator must decide whether the party that answered is acceptable.

today: RFC 4738 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3830. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MIKEY (RFC 3830) has three methods for key transport or exchange: a pre-shared key mode (PSK), a public-key (RSA) mode, and an optional Diffie-Hellman mode. RFC 4650 adds a DH-HMAC mode, for four modes in all. MIKEY is designed for low latency, so every exchange finishes in one-half to one roundtrip, which leaves no room to negotiate the key management protocol's own security parameters.

This document notes that these modes do not cover some common deployments and adds a new one, MIKEY-RSA-R (RSA in Reverse mode). It updates RFC 3830 with this mode.
sections.eli5: MIKEY is a quick way for two phones to agree on a secret code. This adds one more way to do it, for cases the old ways could not handle.

sections.title: Why the Existing Modes Fall Short
sections.content:
The PSK mode needs a secret shared offline, so it does not scale to any-to-any communication. In the RSA mode the Initiator picks the key and encrypts an envelope key with the Responder's public key, so it must know the Responder's ID and certificate (CERT). That breaks when the Responder has several IDs or when its ID changes, as with telephony call forwarding.

The DH and DH-HMAC modes do not need the Responder's identity up front, but they cost more computation and communication, and they are unsuitable for group key distribution. DH-HMAC also needs pre-shared keys between all possible parties.

A second use case is conferencing: invitees ask the convener for group key material by sending a MIKEY I_MESSAGE, so the Initiator asks the Responder for keying material. This fits the MSEC group key management architecture (RFC 4046).
sections.eli5: The old ways need you to know exactly who you are calling, or to have shared a secret ahead of time. That does not work when your call is passed to someone else.

sections.title: How MIKEY-RSA-R Works
sections.content:
The mode takes one full roundtrip. The Initiator sends a signed I_MESSAGE asking the Responder to send the traffic keying material. Either message may carry the sender's certificate or a URL to it. The Responder encrypts the TEK Generation Key (TGK) to the Initiator's public key and sends it in the R_MESSAGE. The Initiator then uses the certificate in the reply to check whether the Responder is really who it wants, and accepts the TGK.

In group use, members request group policy and keys as Initiators from a group key server or sender. Initiators MUST NOT send the SP payload. The Responder sends the payloads needed to distribute the policy and to derive the SRTP session keys: SP, GenExt(CSB_ID), TGK and RAND. In group mode, CSB_ID, RAND and SP in the R_MESSAGE are not optional.
sections.eli5: You send a signed note saying who you are. The other side answers with a locked box holding the secret, and you check their ID before you trust it.

sections.title: The I_MESSAGE
sections.content:
The I_MESSAGE MUST carry the MIKEY HDR and a timestamp payload for replay protection, and it MUST be signed by the Initiator (SIGNi). The HDR holds a CSB_ID chosen randomly by the Initiator, and the V bit MUST be set to 1 because a response is mandatory.

For unicast use, a RAND payload SHOULD be included so the Initiator adds entropy to key derivation. For group use it MAY be included but MUST NOT be used for key generation. IDi and CERTi SHOULD be included, and CERTi MUST match the signing key. If the Initiator will only accept a specific party, it MUST include that identity as IDr.

The Initiator MAY send SP payloads listing the policies it supports. If the Responder supports none, it SHOULD reply with an Error message of type Invalid SPpar (error 10). A Responder that cannot parse the message SHOULD send error 13, and RFC 3830 implementations MAY return error 12 instead. The Responder MUST send an R_MESSAGE if SIGNi verifies and the timestamp is current.
sections.eli5: The first note must say when it was written and carry a signature, so nobody can fake it or replay it later.

sections.title: The R_MESSAGE
sections.content:
The R_MESSAGE reuses the I_MESSAGE's CSB_ID. For group keys the Responder MUST add a General Extension payload with a new CSB_ID, so all members compute keys from the same value. That payload MUST NOT appear in unicast. The T payload is copied from the I_MESSAGE. In unicast, exactly one side supplies RAND: if the I_MESSAGE had one, the R_MESSAGE MUST NOT, and otherwise it MUST. In group use the Responder always sends RAND.

The KEMAC payload holds the Responder's identity and the TGK, encrypted, followed by a MAC. Both keys come from a random envelope key, env_key, which the PKE payload carries encrypted with the Initiator's public key. The Responder signs the message plus IDi, IDr and T in SIGNr.

The Initiator MUST silently discard an R_MESSAGE whose RAND presence does not match its own message, or whose SP payload contains a policy it did not offer.
sections.eli5: The reply holds the secret in a box that only you can open. A seal proves who made it. If it looks wrong, you ignore it without saying anything.

sections.title: Certificate Handling
sections.content:
If a certificate payload is present, the X.509v3 URL Cert type is the default and MUST be implemented. HTTP URLs (RFC 2585) MUST be supported; FTP URLs are not required. DER-encoded X.509 certificates with the application/pkix-cert MIME type MUST be supported.

The RECOMMENDED validation method is OCSP (RFC 2560). When the response has a nextUpdate time, it limits how long the certificate may be cached; otherwise the timeout is local policy.
sections.eli5: The ID card can be sent along or fetched from a web address, and it should be checked to see that it is still valid.

sections.title: When to Use RSA-R or RSA
sections.content:
RSA-R suits cases where the Responder may differ from the party the message was sent to, as when a call is retargeted or forwarded. It also suits conferences where the Initiator wants the Responder to supply all the keying material, similar to group key download in GDOI, GSAKMP and GKDP.

The plain RSA mode is better when the Initiator already knows the Responder's identity and CERT, when switching an existing session from non-secure to secure, or when only the targeted Responder is acceptable. One limit: RSA-R may not easily support 3-way calling, which can need an extra message, although a conference bridge avoids the problem.
sections.eli5: Use the new way when your call might get passed to someone else. Use the old way when you already know exactly who you are talking to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The signed I_MESSAGE assures the Responder that the Initiator made it, and the timestamp shows it is live. Checking signatures costs the Responder computing effort, so caching recently verified requests can reduce denial-of-service risk. Since nothing in the I_MESSAGE is encrypted to the Responder, its DoS properties match the DH method rather than the public-key method.

Because the Responder may differ from the intended party, the Initiator is responsible for judging whether its identity is acceptable under local policy, for example by strong authentication, a blacklist or a whitelist. When both unicast and multicast streams are needed, using multiple RSA-R instances is RECOMMENDED over one group-mode instance, to avoid key reuse with counter mode.

For unicast, Initiator and Responder both contribute randomness (RAND from one side, TGK from the other). MIKEY needs synchronized clocks, so a secure clock synchronization protocol SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: Because the person who answers may not be who you expected, you have to decide if you are happy with them before using the secret.
